nameStory: The Atlantic wolffish gets its fearsome name from its impressive set of teeth - large, prominent canine teeth at the front of its mouth that look remarkably like a wolf's fangs. These powerful chompers aren't just for show; they're perfectly designed for crushing the hard shells of sea urchins, crabs, and mollusks that make up the wolffish's diet. The 'wolf of the sea' is a fitting name for this toothy predator of New England's cold waters.
description: The Atlantic wolffish is a large, eel-like fish with a big head and an intimidating set of teeth that would make any wolf jealous. These bottom-dwelling fish can grow quite large, with their long, muscular bodies perfectly suited for life on the seafloor. They have a distinctive appearance with their blunt snout, small eyes, and that unforgettable toothy grin. Despite their scary appearance, they're actually quite docile unless threatened, spending most of their time hunting for shellfish and sea urchins in the cold depths.

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large, prominent canine teeth at the front of the mouth that protrude even when closed, giving it a wolf-like appearance. The teeth feel incredibly hard and sharp if you ever handle one.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Long, eel-like body that feels muscular and solid to the touch, with a large, blunt head that's disproportionately big compared to the tapering tail section.

idTips.label: Fins
idTips.description: Long, continuous dorsal fin running along most of the back, and no pelvic fins at all - this gives them a distinctly different silhouette from most other fish.

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Typically dark gray to brownish with darker vertical bars or blotches along the sides, though color can vary. The skin feels smooth and slightly slimy when handled.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can grow to impressive sizes, with adults commonly reaching several feet in length. They feel surprisingly heavy and solid when lifted.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in very cold, deep waters along rocky bottoms where they hunt for sea urchins and crabs. Rarely seen in shallow water or warm areas.

habitat: Atlantic wolffish live in the cold, deep waters off New England's coast, typically staying near rocky bottoms where they can hunt for their favorite prey. They prefer areas with plenty of sea urchins, crabs, and mollusks to crunch on with those powerful teeth. You're most likely to encounter one if you're deep-sea fishing or if one gets brought up as bycatch by commercial fishermen working the offshore waters.

seasonality.spring: Wolffish may move to slightly different depths as water temperatures begin to change, but they're rarely observed by casual anglers during this season.
seasonality.summer: Most active feeding period, though still in deep waters. Any wolffish caught during summer fishing will be in peak condition with full bellies.
seasonality.fall: Breeding season begins, with both male and female wolffish participating in caring for their unusually large eggs on the seafloor.
seasonality.winter: Their natural antifreeze proteins keep them active in the coldest waters when most other fish have moved to warmer areas or become sluggish.

funFact: Atlantic wolffish produce their own antifreeze proteins in their blood to survive in waters so cold they would literally freeze other fish solid - it's like having biological winter windshield washer fluid running through their veins!
confusionNotes: With their eel-like body, wolffish might be confused with large eels, but those massive protruding teeth are a dead giveaway - no eel has anything close to those wolf-like fangs. Remember: if it looks like an eel that could bite your finger off, it's probably a wolffish!
contextualKnowledge: Despite names like 'devil fish' and 'wolf eel,' Atlantic wolffish are actually quite docile and are not aggressive toward humans unless handled roughly. The 'catfish' part of some of their common names is misleading - they're not related to freshwater catfish at all.
compareHints: Since Atlantic wolffish is the only member of its genus in New England waters, it's quite distinctive among local fish species. The combination of the eel-like body, massive protruding teeth, and preference for very cold, deep water makes it unlike any other fish you'll encounter in the region. No other New England fish has that characteristic wolf-like dental arrangement.
